blocks.text: “A 48-year-old woman complains of urine leakage when coughing and also experiences sudden urges to urinate. Take a focused history and discuss management.”
“A patient has both stress and urgency urinary incontinence. Explain how you would assess and manage her.”
“Counsel a woman with mixed urinary incontinence who has not improved with initial treatment.”
“Discuss the role of pelvic floor training, bladder training and surgery in mixed urinary incontinence.”

Main OSCE objective: Recognise that the patient has both stress and urgency components, determine which component is most bothersome, exclude other causes and develop a treatment plan that addresses both.
Mixed urinary incontinence (MUI) is the involuntary leakage of urine associated with both:
Stress urinary incontinence: leakage during coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting or physical exertion.
Urgency urinary incontinence: leakage associated with, or immediately preceded by, a sudden compelling urge to urinate that is difficult to defer.
A woman may experience both types equally, or one may be substantially more troublesome than the other.
Key examination principle: Treatment should be guided by the patient's symptoms, preferences and the relative contribution of each component.
Mixed urinary incontinence involves a combination of mechanisms.
Weakness of urethral support or impaired urethral sphincter function permits urine leakage when abdominal pressure rises.
Abnormal bladder storage sensations and urgency lead to a sudden desire to void, sometimes followed by involuntary detrusor contraction and leakage.

The two components may coexist because of age-related changes, childbirth-related pelvic floor injury, neurological factors or other urinary tract conditions. Urodynamic detrusor overactivity is not required to diagnose the urgency component clinically.
Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain that you will ask about urinary leakage, triggers, urgency and the impact on daily life.
Obtain consent.
Ensure privacy and offer a chaperone if an intimate examination is indicated.
Explain any proposed examination or investigations and invite questions.
Example:

“Hello, I understand that you have been experiencing urine leakage in different situations. I would like to ask when it happens, whether you experience a sudden urge to urinate, and how the symptoms affect you. This will help us identify the different components and choose suitable treatment. Is that alright?”
Begin with an open question:
“Can you tell me about the urine leakage you have been experiencing?”
Establish:
Onset and duration.
Frequency and progression.
Severity and amount of leakage.
Whether symptoms began together or at different times.
Previous treatments and response.
Ask whether leakage occurs during:
Coughing.
Sneezing.
Laughing.
Running, jumping or exercise.
Lifting heavy objects.
Standing or changing position.
Clarify whether the leakage is a few drops or a large amount and whether it requires pads or a change of clothing.
Typical finding: Urine leaks synchronously with coughing or physical exertion, usually without a preceding compelling urge.
Ask:
Do you experience a sudden, compelling need to urinate?
Is it difficult to postpone urination?
Do you leak before reaching the toilet?
Do you experience urgency when hearing running water or arriving home?
How often do you pass urine during the day?
How many times do you wake at night to urinate?
Typical finding: Sudden urgency followed by leakage before the patient reaches the toilet.
This is one of the most important aspects of the station.
Ask:

items: “Which type of leakage bothers you the most?”

blocks.text: “Are you more troubled by leakage during coughing and exercise, or by the sudden urge to urinate?”

items: “Which symptom interferes most with your daily activities?”

blocks.text: “If we could improve one symptom first, which would you choose?”
The answer helps guide the order of treatment. Do not assume that the stress component is more important simply because it is easier to demonstrate during examination.
Ask about:
Dysuria.
Haematuria.
Suprapubic pain.
Recurrent urinary tract infections.
Frequency and nocturia.
Hesitancy or weak urinary stream.
Straining to void.
Incomplete bladder emptying.
Continuous leakage.
These symptoms may indicate infection, retention, another bladder disorder or a fistula rather than uncomplicated mixed incontinence alone.
Ask about:
Number of pregnancies and deliveries.
Vaginal, instrumental and caesarean deliveries.
Prolonged labour or obstetric trauma.
Birth of large babies.
Previous pelvic organ prolapse.
Previous hysterectomy or pelvic surgery.
Menopausal symptoms.
Vaginal dryness or irritation.
Previous continence procedures.
Plans for future pregnancy.
Ask about:
Diabetes mellitus.
Neurological disorders, such as stroke, multiple sclerosis or spinal disease.
Obesity.
Chronic cough.
Constipation.
Mobility difficulties.
Diuretic use and other relevant medications.
Previous pelvic radiotherapy.

content_groups.group_title: H. Impact on quality of life

blocks.text: Explore the effects on:
Exercise and work.
Sleep and nocturia.
Travel and social activities.
Sexual relationships.
Clothing choices and pad use.
Confidence and emotional well-being.
Ask specifically about:
Visible or persistent haematuria.
Recurrent unexplained urinary infections.
Persistent pelvic or bladder pain.
Difficulty emptying the bladder.
Continuous leakage.
New neurological symptoms, including leg weakness or saddle sensory loss.
New neurological deficits with acute urinary retention require urgent assessment.
Assess:
General appearance and mobility.
Body mass index where relevant.
Abdominal masses or distension.
A palpable bladder or suprapubic tenderness.
Relevant neurological findings when indicated.
With informed consent and an appropriate chaperone:
Inspect vulval and vaginal tissues.
Look for atrophy, irritation or other abnormalities.
Assess for pelvic organ prolapse.
Assess pelvic floor contraction strength, endurance and coordination.
Look for visible urethral leakage during a cough stress test if appropriate.
Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Ask the patient to have a comfortably full bladder.
Position her appropriately.
Ask her to cough forcefully.
Observe for leakage from the urethral meatus.
Repeat in the standing position if clinically appropriate and the initial test is negative despite a convincing history.
Positive result: Visible leakage synchronous with coughing supports the stress component.
A negative test does not exclude stress incontinence.

Ask the patient to squeeze and lift the pelvic floor as if preventing passage of wind. Check whether she can contract and relax correctly. If contraction is weak or poorly coordinated, supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy may be particularly useful.

rows: Pure stress urinary incontinence
Leakage with exertion without urgency-related leakage
Pure urgency urinary incontinence
Leakage associated with a compelling urge, without stress-related leakage
Urinary tract infection
Dysuria, suprapubic pain or acute worsening of urgency and frequency
Overflow incontinence
Retention, weak stream, incomplete emptying or dribbling
Diabetes mellitus
Polyuria and polydipsia, often with large urine volumes
Vesicovaginal fistula
Continuous watery leakage, often following pelvic surgery or obstructed labour
Pelvic organ prolapse
Vaginal bulge or pelvic pressure, sometimes associated with urinary dysfunction
Neurological bladder dysfunction
Relevant neurological history or abnormal neurological examination
Urinalysis
Initial assessment for blood, glucose and evidence of infection
Urine culture
When infection is suspected
Bladder diary for at least 3 days
Records fluid intake, voiding, urgency, leakage and nocturia
Post-void residual measurement
If there is voiding difficulty, suspected retention, recurrent infection or relevant neurological disease
Urodynamic studies
Selected cases with diagnostic uncertainty or complex symptoms, particularly when results may change treatment
Cystoscopy or imaging
Only for specific indications, not routinely in uncomplicated mixed incontinence

blocks.text: A bladder diary can help identify whether the urgency or stress component occurs more frequently and can establish a baseline for monitoring treatment response.
Treatment is individualised and usually begins with conservative measures that can improve both components.
Particularly important for the stress component. Offer a supervised programme for at least 3 months, with correct technique and progressive training.
Particularly important for the urgency component. Use a bladder diary, planned voiding intervals and urgency-suppression strategies.
Encourage weight management if indicated, appropriate hydration, reduction of caffeine if it triggers urgency, and treatment of constipation or chronic cough.
Explain the squeeze-and-lift action around the vagina and anus.
Check that the patient is not simply contracting her buttocks or holding her breath.
Teach sustained and quick contractions, tailored to her ability.
Encourage consistent practice and functional contractions before coughing or lifting.
Arrange supervised review to assess technique and progress.
If she cannot identify the correct muscles, refer for supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy.
Record baseline voiding intervals in a diary.
Set a manageable voiding schedule.
Gradually lengthen intervals as tolerated.
When urgency occurs, pause, breathe slowly, relax and perform a few quick pelvic floor contractions if able.
Once the urge settles, walk calmly to the toilet.
Review progress and modify the plan as needed.
Avoid severe fluid restriction or forcing the patient to delay voiding when it causes pain.

content_groups.group_title: D. Pharmacological treatment for the urgency component

blocks.text: If urgency remains troublesome despite behavioural measures, consider medication based on the patient's risks, preferences and local availability.

Antimuscarinics include oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin and trospium. Potential adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention and cognitive effects in susceptible patients.
Beta-3 agonists include mirabegron and, where available, vibegron. Mirabegron may increase blood pressure, so blood pressure and contraindications should be reviewed.
These medicines target urgency symptoms; they do not correct urethral support failure responsible for the stress component.

content_groups.group_title: E. Management when stress symptoms predominate

blocks.text: If stress leakage is the main concern:
Prioritise supervised pelvic floor muscle training.
Address weight and other relevant risk factors.
Consider continence pessaries or other support devices in selected patients.
Refer for specialist assessment if symptoms remain troublesome.

Surgical options for appropriately selected patients may include a midurethral sling, colposuspension or autologous fascial sling. The benefits, risks, alternatives and possibility of persistent or recurrent symptoms must be discussed.

content_groups.group_title: F. Management when urgency symptoms predominate

blocks.text: If urgency leakage is the main concern:
Prioritise bladder training.
Modify relevant fluid and dietary triggers.
Consider pharmacological treatment if needed.
Refer for specialist management if symptoms remain refractory or diagnosis is uncertain.
Advanced treatments such as intradetrusor botulinum toxin, sacral neuromodulation or tibial nerve stimulation may be considered by specialists in selected cases.

content_groups.group_title: G. If both components are equally troublesome

blocks.text: Use a combined plan addressing both stress and urgency symptoms. Review progress separately for each component, because one may improve while the other persists.

Important: Do not automatically recommend stress-incontinence surgery as the first step in a patient whose urgency component is severe or poorly characterised. Surgery may improve stress leakage but does not reliably resolve urgency symptoms.
A possible OSCE response:

“Your symptoms suggest that you have mixed urinary incontinence. This means urine leaks both when pressure increases, such as during coughing or exercise, and when you experience a sudden urge to pass urine.

The two types can respond to different treatments. Pelvic floor muscle training can help the stress component, while bladder training and certain medicines can help the urgency component. We will first establish which symptoms bother you most and check for infection or other causes.

We can begin with a combined conservative programme and review your progress. If the symptoms remain troublesome, we can discuss additional treatments or referral to a specialist. The aim is to improve your continence and quality of life while choosing options that suit your preferences.”
Check the patient's understanding and ask which symptom she would most like to improve.

subsections.subsection_title: How to report findings in an OSCE

content_groups.group_title: Example A: Mixed incontinence with stress predominance

blocks.text: “This patient reports leakage during coughing and exercise, together with occasional urgency-related leakage before reaching the toilet. The stress component appears more troublesome. Abdominal examination is unremarkable, and the cough stress test demonstrates leakage synchronous with coughing. The history is consistent with mixed urinary incontinence, with stress predominance. I would arrange urinalysis, assess pelvic floor function, obtain a bladder diary and offer supervised pelvic floor muscle training alongside bladder training.”

content_groups.group_title: Example B: Mixed incontinence with urgency predominance

blocks.text: “This patient reports frequent urgency, nocturia and leakage before reaching the toilet, with occasional leakage during coughing. The urgency component is more bothersome. I would investigate reversible causes, perform urinalysis, review fluid intake and medications, obtain a bladder diary and prioritise bladder training while also addressing the stress component.”

content_groups.group_title: Example C: Possible complicated urinary dysfunction

blocks.text: “This patient reports mixed leakage but also has a weak urinary stream and a sensation of incomplete emptying. These symptoms raise concern for voiding dysfunction or retention. I would assess the post-void residual volume and arrange further evaluation before prescribing treatment that could worsen retention or proceeding to surgery.”
Q1. Define mixed urinary incontinence.
Involuntary urine leakage associated with both stress-related activities and urgency.
Q2. How do you determine which component predominates?
Ask about the frequency, severity and impact of each type of leakage, and review a bladder diary.
Q3. What is the first-line management?
A combined conservative approach: supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months, bladder training, and appropriate lifestyle interventions.
Q4. Will antimuscarinics treat the stress component?
No. They target urgency symptoms rather than urethral support failure.
Q5. Will surgery for stress incontinence cure the urgency component?
Not reliably. Stress surgery primarily targets stress leakage; urgency symptoms may persist and require separate treatment.
Q6. What is the role of urodynamic testing?
It is not routinely required for every patient. It may be appropriate in complex cases or when diagnostic findings could change treatment decisions, particularly before certain procedures.
Q7. What complications should be discussed before midurethral sling surgery?

Potential complications include bladder or urethral injury, bleeding, infection, mesh exposure, pain, voiding dysfunction, urgency symptoms and recurrent incontinence. Risks depend on the procedure and patient.
Q8. What symptoms require further investigation?
Haematuria, persistent pain, recurrent unexplained infections, continuous leakage, significant voiding difficulty or new neurological symptoms.
Q9. How do you assess treatment success?
Compare the baseline and follow-up bladder diary, frequency of leakage, pad use, urgency episodes and the patient's reported quality of life.
Q10. What if the patient has a plan for future pregnancy?
Discuss this before considering surgery because future pregnancy and childbirth may affect long-term continence outcomes. Conservative treatment is generally prioritised where appropriate.
Recognising only one component and missing the other.
Failing to ask which symptom is most troublesome.
Treating all mixed incontinence as though it were purely stress incontinence.
Prescribing urgency medication without considering retention risk or contraindications.
Assuming stress surgery will cure urgency symptoms.
Failing to screen for infection, haematuria or neurological red flags.
Forgetting to document baseline symptoms before treatment.
Failing to discuss the patient's preferences and quality-of-life goals.
M — Mixed triggers: exertion and urgency.
I — Identify the predominant symptom.
X — eXclude infection and other causes.
E — Examine pelvic floor function and assess appropriately.
D — Dual treatment: pelvic floor training plus bladder training, with further treatment as needed.
